answer_text:
Let

\[
f(z)=\frac{z}{\sin(\pi z^2)}.
\]

Poles occur where \(\sin(\pi z^2)=0\). Since

\[
\sin(\pi z^2)=0 \iff \pi z^2=k\pi \iff z^2=k,\qquad k\in\mathbb Z,
\]

the relevant points are \(z=0\), \(z=\pm\sqrt n\), and \(z=\pm i\sqrt n\) for \(n\in\mathbb Z^+\).

---

### 1. At \(z=0\)

Near \(z=0\),

\[
\sin(\pi z^2)=\pi z^2-\frac{\pi^3 z^6}{6}+O(z^{10}).
\]

Thus

\[
f(z)=\frac{z}{\pi z^2\left(1-\frac{\pi^2z^4}{6}+O(z^8)\right)}
=\frac{1}{\pi z}\left(1+O(z^4)\right).
\]

So the principal part has a single \(z^{-1}\) term. Therefore \(z=0\) is a **simple pole**, i.e. a pole of order \(1\).

---

### 2. At \(z=\pm\sqrt n\)

Let \(z_0=\pm\sqrt n\). Then

\[
\sin(\pi z_0^2)=\sin(\pi n)=0.
\]

Consider the denominator

\[
D(z)=\sin(\pi z^2).
\]

Its derivative is

\[
D'(z)=2\pi z\cos(\pi z^2).
\]

At \(z_0=\pm\sqrt n\),

\[
D'(z_0)=2\pi z_0\cos(\pi n)=2\pi z_0(-1)^n\neq 0.
\]

So \(D(z)\) has a simple zero at \(z_0\). Since the numerator \(z\) is nonzero there, \(f\) has a simple pole at each \(z=\pm\sqrt n\).

---

### 3. At \(z=\pm i\sqrt n\)

Let \(z_0=\pm i\sqrt n\). Then

\[
z_0^2=-n,
\]

so

\[
\sin(\pi z_0^2)=\sin(-\pi n)=0.
\]

Again,

\[
D'(z_0)=2\pi z_0\cos(\pi z_0^2)
=2\pi z_0\cos(-\pi n)
=2\pi z_0(-1)^n\neq 0.
\]

Thus \(D(z)\) has a simple zero at \(z_0\), while the numerator \(z\) is nonzero. Hence each \(z=\pm i\sqrt n\) is also a simple pole.

---

Therefore, all the listed points are simple poles:

\[
\boxed{
\begin{array}{c|c}
z & \text{order of pole} \\
\hline
0 & 1 \\
\pm\sqrt n & 1 \\
\pm i\sqrt n & 1
\end{array}
}
\]
